title: Power-Up Multipliers
story: In your card game, each player holds a row of power-up cards with multipliers: 3 triples your score, -1 flips it negative, 0 wipes it out. Your multiplier is all the cards multiplied together.

Before each turn the game discards one card, and under every card it shows the multiplier if that card were discarded. Dividing the full product by a card breaks as soon as a card is 0, so the scoring code only multiplies.
task: Write withoutEach(cards). Return a list out of the same length where out[i] is the product of every card except cards[i].
Do not use division. Aim for O(n) time.
constraints: The product of all the non-zero cards fits in a 32-bit signed integer.

examples.explanation: Discarding the 2 leaves 3 × 4 × 5 = 60, discarding the 3 leaves 2 × 4 × 5 = 40, discarding the 4 leaves 2 × 3 × 5 = 30, and discarding the 5 leaves 2 × 3 × 4 = 24.
Every product that still contains the 0 is 0. Discarding the 0 gives 3 × 2 × (-1) = -6. Dividing the full product, which is 0, by the 0 card would fail here.

hints: In [2, 3, 4, 5], the answer under the 4 is 2 × 3 × 5. Which of those cards are left of the 4, and which right?
Every answer is (product of cards to the left) × (product of cards to the right). For the first card, the left side is empty and counts as 1.
The left products for every position can be built in one left-to-right pass, each from the previous one. The right products work the same way from the other end.

Fill out[i] with the product of everything before i, using a running product that starts at 1. Then walk from the right with a second running product, starting at 1: multiply out[i] by it, then multiply it by cards[i].
bruteForce: For each position, multiply all the other cards together.

That takes O(n²) time, about 10 billion multiplications for 100,000 cards, because neighbouring answers share most of their factors and the brute force recomputes them each time. Dividing the full product by each card would be O(n), but it fails when a card is 0 and is not allowed here.

js: * @return {number[]} out[i] = product of all cards except cards[i]

tests.note: two cards: each answer is the other card
one zero at the end: defeats total / card

js: let left = 1; // product of cards before i
let right = 1; // product of cards after i
py: left = 1  # product of cards before i
right = 1  # product of cards after i
walkthrough: Removing card i splits the row into the cards before it and the cards after it. The answer is the product of the two parts, and each can be built one card at a time, like a running sum.
• The left pass writes the product of everything before each card, giving out = [1, 2, 6, 24]. The first entry is 1 because nothing comes before it, and the later entries are 2, 2 × 3 and 2 × 3 × 4.
• The right pass starts with right = 1. At index 3, out[3] = 24 × 1 = 24, and then right becomes 5.
• At index 0, out[0] = 1 × 60 = 60, so the result is [60, 40, 30, 24].

In each pass, write the answer before multiplying in the current card, which keeps card i out of its own answer. Zeros need no special case, because a zero simply makes the running product 0 for every position after it.
solution.timeWhy: Two passes over the cards, with constant work per card.
solution.spaceWhy: Apart from the output list, only two running products are kept.
solution.takeaway: The product of everything except position i is the product of everything before i times the product of everything after i. Build both with running totals from each end, using prefix and suffix products here, and each answer then costs O(1).
